newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks seen racing higher on budget bounce.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks seen racing higher on budget bounce.

text.p: Bulls stampeding through Indian equity markets in the wake of a pro-growth, pro-investment budget are likely to drive share values still higher next week, traders said on Sunday.
"There may be some ups and downs, but we can safely say that the index is now headed higher," Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at brokerage Kotak Securities, told Reuters.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget unveiled late on Friday announced sharp cuts in corporate and income taxes, allowed firms to buy back shares and raised limits on foreign institutional investment in some firms.
Stock prices zoomed to dizzy heights in euphoric buying during two special post-budget sessions on Friday evening and Saturday.

On Saturday, the Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-share index staged a 5.63 percent gain, following a five percent jump on Friday. The index ended Saturday with a net gain of 418 points, or nearly 12 percent, on the week, closing at 3,857.49.
"A lot of it (buying) is sentiment-driven. Foreign funds who have been waiting should also pump in money," said M.R. Madhavan, market strategist at ICICI Securities & Finance Company.
"The mood is very buoyant. The finance minister has done an excellent job in taking the (liberalisation) baton forward," said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at Lloyds Securities.

The government diluted a controversial minimum tax announced in the 1996/97 budget last July and raised the investment limit for foreign institutional investors in some firms to 30 percent from 24 percent.
The freeing of the investment limit will likely stoke demand for blue chips, said dealers who described the budget as ground-breaking and a gift to the market.
The tax rate on domestic firms was reduced to 35 percent from 40 percent, and on foreign firms to 48 percent from 55 percent.
The proposed budget, which must be approved by parliament, also abolished a tax on income from dividends and trimmed import duties.
"This is a sustained bull run that has been started. The major factor is the substantial reduction in tax rates," said dealer Govind Agarwal at brokerage Motilal Oswal.

Before the budget, analysts were only cautiously optimistic that the fractious 15-party centre-left goverment would be able to push through market reforms needed to kick-start a slowing economy and rebuild investor confidence.

"Happy days are here again. The budget brings back the prodigal Indian investor to contribute to the process of vital capital formation," said A.K.T. Janak, president of the investment banking division at Apple Finance Ltd.
Still, some analysts said the market might take a breather and book profits, although the undertone remained bullish.
"When people start looking at some negatives, the market should react. Many small investors are holding on to stocks with huge losses over the past two years," said I-Sec's Madhavan.
